newsitem.title: USA: Ill. electric deregulation put off to fall session.
newsitem.headline: Ill. electric deregulation put off to fall session.

text.p: Illinois electric utility deregulation legislation has been delayed until the fall to give lawmakers more time to ensure that a massive bill completed in the just-concluded session does as intended, a sponsor said Monday.

"We needed more time to ensure that some basic principles we have are in the bill," Sen. William Mahar, R-Orland Park, said. "The bill is so technical that one lawyer will say they are in there and another will say they are not."

Illinois representatives voted overwhelmingly to approve the deregulation plan on Friday, but a midnight Saturday deadline to complete a state budget and other major funding issues led senators to wait until the fall veto session to take up the deregulation bill.
Mahar said the bill must guarantee rate decreases for consumers and still allow future amendment. The bill has been in negotiation for a long time, he added.
"I was very disappointed we didn't get the thing done, but on an issue of this importance, it is important to do it right the first time," Mahar said.

Bill supporters included Commonwealth Edison, a subsidiary of Unicom Corp ; Illinois Power Co, a subsidiary of Illinova Corp ; Central Illinois Public Service Corp; the Citizens Utility Board; the Illinois Retail Merchants Association; and the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers.
Commonwealth Edison spokeswoman Marjorie Benzkofer said Monday the utility was extremely disappointed that the General Assembly did not act on the deregulation plan.
"It was an issue that could have and should have been handled this session," Benzkofer said. "Illinois consumers shouldn't have been denied deregulation until the fall."
Central Illinois Light, a subsidiary of CILCORP, and the Illinois Manufacturer's Association opposed it.
The legislation provided for residential rate cuts of from 5 percent to 15 percent beginning in 1998.

The bill phased in residential customer choice of utility beginning in the year 2000 and finishing in 2002. All commercial/industrial customers would be given a choice by 2000, with large industrial customers beginning in October 1999.
The plan also called for partial recovery for investments made during the regulatory environment that may not be recoverable under competition, referred to in the industry as "stranded costs."

The bill also provided $76 million of state funding for low income customers, $100 million for development of renewable energy resources over 10 years from customer surcharges and $30 million for energy efficiency projects over 10 years paid by the utilities.
Rep. J. Philip Novak, D-Bradley, and Rep. Vincent Persico, R-Glen Ellyn, sponsored the measure in the House.
